history.heading: Colonial era
paragraphs: Nicaragua, the largest country in Central America, was home to Nahua-speaking peoples on the Pacific side, from whose chief Nicarao the name may derive, and to Miskito and other peoples on the Caribbean coast. Spain conquered the Pacific region from 1524, founding Granada and León, while Britain held influence over the Mosquito Coast.

history.heading: Independence and US intervention
paragraphs: Nicaragua became independent in 1821 and fully separate in 1838. Rivalry between liberal León and conservative Granada led to civil wars. In 1856 the American adventurer William Walker made himself president before being driven out. The United States occupied Nicaragua from 1912 to 1933, resisted by Augusto César Sandino.
Anastasio Somoza García, head of the US-trained National Guard, had Sandino killed in 1934 and founded a family dictatorship that lasted until 1979.

history.heading: Revolution and after
paragraphs: The Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) overthrew the Somoza regime in 1979. The Sandinista government, led by Daniel Ortega, faced the US-backed Contra rebels in a war that killed around 30,000 people. In 1990 Violeta Chamorro defeated Ortega in elections.

Ortega returned to power in 2007. In 2018 protests against social security reforms were violently suppressed, killing over 300 people. Since then, the government has jailed or exiled opposition leaders, closed thousands of NGOs and universities, and stripped critics of citizenship.

culture.heading: Poetry and traditions
paragraphs: Spanish is the official language, and English Creole, Miskito and other languages are spoken on the Caribbean coast. Most people are Catholic, with a growing evangelical population.

Nicaragua is known as a land of poets; Rubén Darío founded the modernismo literary movement. El Güegüense, a satirical drama, is recognised by UNESCO. Gallo pinto (rice and beans) is the national dish. Baseball is the most popular sport.

politics.heading: Authoritarian rule
paragraphs: Nicaragua is formally a presidential republic, but power is concentrated in President Daniel Ortega and his wife Rosario Murillo. A 2025 constitutional reform made them "co-presidents" and extended the presidential term to six years. Elections in 2021 were held after main opposition candidates were jailed, and are not recognised as free by many countries.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Nicaragua is one of the poorest countries in the Americas. Exports include gold, coffee, beef, textiles from free trade zones, sugar and seafood. Remittances from Nicaraguans in the US, Costa Rica and Spain have grown to a large share of GDP as many people emigrated after 2018.
